title: Record gold prices outpace rising mining costs in Q1’26
gist: Global gold AISC rose 16% y/y to a record US$1,785/oz in Q1'26 — the 28th straight y/y increase — driven mainly by gold-price-linked royalties (now 12% of AISC vs ~6% five years ago) and by fuel/freight inflation from the Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz closure. Yet a 70% y/y gold price rise (peak US$5,595/oz) pushed average AISC margins to a record US$3,076/oz, funding record FCF, net-cash balance sheets and large buybacks; the squeeze comes in Q2'26 as prices fell 7.2% q/q while the late-quarter cost shock fully lands.

themes.theme: Royalties as the new structural cost line

insights.claim: Global average gold producer All-In Sustaining Costs rose 5% q/q and 16% y/y to US$1,785/oz in Q1'26, marking the 28th consecutive year-on-year increase in AISC.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Cost inflation in gold mining is structural, not cyclical — model AISC as a permanently rising floor, so any gold price plateau compresses miner margins mechanically.
insights.quote: Rising costs have become a persistent feature of the industry, with the quarter marking the 28th consecutive year-on-year increase in AISC.
insights.locator: 2026 started in dramatic fashion, as record

insights.claim: Royalty payments to governments were the single largest driver of the Q1'26 AISC increase, climbing 24% q/q and 85% y/y as record revenues fed price-linked state take.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Royalties, not diesel or labour, are the marginal cost driver in a gold bull market — the sensitivity that matters for miner earnings models is fiscal, not operational.
insights.locator: Numerous cost drivers contributed to the increase

insights.claim: Royalties doubled their share of the average gold operation's cost base from approximately 6% of AISC in Q1'21 to 12% in Q1'26.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: A doubling in five years means each further dollar of gold upside is taxed roughly twice as hard as in the last cycle — haircut the price-to-margin beta in miner valuations.
insights.quote: In Q1’21, royalties accounted for approximately 6% of AISC. By Q1’26, this share had doubled to 12% of the average operation’s cost base.
insights.locator: When compared with five years previous

insights.claim: West African states have replaced flat royalties with gold-price-linked sliding scales — Ghana in March 2026 (up to 12% above US$4,500/oz, replacing a flat 5%), Burkina Faso in 2025 (10% at US$4,000-4,500/oz) and Mali in 2024 (9.5% at US$4,100/oz).
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Sliding scales cap investor participation in gold rallies for West African assets — price a structurally lower margin ceiling into Ghana/Burkina/Mali-exposed producers versus Nevada or Australia peers.
insights.quote: The scale is linked to the gold price and can reach rates of 12% when prices exceed US$4,500/oz.
insights.locator: Ghana introduced a new sliding scale royalty system

insights.claim: At IAMGOLD's Essakane mine in Burkina Faso, royalty costs surged 220% y/y and reached 35% of cash costs in Q1'26.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: A single-asset illustration of how resource nationalism can consume a third of a mine's cash cost base — screen for producers with concentrated West African exposure.
insights.quote: royalty costs surged by 220% y/y, accounting for 35% of cash costs
insights.locator: For example, at IAMGOLD’s Essakane mine

insights.claim: Resolute Mining flagged higher royalties as a key reason costs at its Syama mine exceeded guidance in Q1'26.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Guidance misses attributable to fiscal changes rather than operations signal that consensus cost models have not yet caught up with new royalty regimes.
insights.locator: Resolute Mining also identified higher royalties

insights.claim: The cost impact of rising royalties is explicitly non-uniform across the industry because fiscal regimes and the degree of resource nationalism differ by jurisdiction.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Jurisdiction, not orebody grade, is becoming the primary dispersion factor in gold miner margins — a basis for long-safe-jurisdiction / short-high-royalty pair trades.
insights.quote: However, the effect was not uniform across the industry. Differences in fiscal regimes, combined with rising resource nationalism, accentuated the impact in some jurisdictions.
insights.locator: However, the effect was not uniform

themes.theme: Iran war and the Hormuz energy shock

insights.claim: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and damage to Middle East energy infrastructure disrupted global supply chains, raising gold miners' fuel, power, freight, shipping and consumable costs in Q1'26.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Geopolitical energy shocks transmit into mining cost curves within a single quarter — watch Hormuz status as a direct input to gold miner margin forecasts, not just to the gold price.
insights.locator: The Cost of Conflict

insights.claim: Diesel price shocks were highly regional in Q1'26: average US diesel ended the quarter 54% higher q/q while wholesale diesel in Perth, Australia rose 96% over the quarter.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: The near-doubling of Australian diesel versus a 54% US move means Western Australian producers carry roughly twice the fuel-cost shock of North American peers — a regional cost dispersion trade.
insights.quote: The average diesel price in the US ended the quarter 54% higher q/q, while wholesale diesel prices in Perth, Australia increased by 96% over the quarter.
insights.locator: Fuel and power were among the largest concerns

insights.claim: Some smaller Western Australian gold operations reportedly suspended activity outright because of fuel constraints during Q1'26.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Physical fuel availability — not just price — became a production-stoppage risk for juniors; expect Q2 production misses concentrated among small WA producers.
insights.quote: some smaller operations reportedly suspending activity because of fuel constraints
insights.locator: Western Australian miners came under particularly significant pressure

insights.claim: Bunker fuel costs doubled in early March 2026 and war risk insurance premiums rose, feeding through to miners via imported consumables and spare parts.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Freight and insurance are a second, lagged transmission channel into mining costs — the cost impulse keeps arriving even after spot energy prices stabilise.
insights.quote: Bunker fuel costs doubled in early March, while war risk insurance premiums increased.
insights.locator: Broader Supply-Chain Pressures

insights.claim: Gold Fields recorded a 40% rise in freight and consumables costs since the start of the Iran war in its Q1'26 report.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: A hard, company-level magnitude for the war's cost pass-through — use ~40% on freight/consumables as a benchmark when stress-testing other producers' Q2 costs.
insights.quote: Gold Fields recorded a 40% rise in freight and consumables costs since the start of the Iran war
insights.locator: In their Q1’26 report, Gold Fields recorded

insights.claim: Disruption to natural gas and ammonia markets raised prices for explosives and sodium cyanide, while rising aluminium prices lifted the cost of maintenance materials and replacement parts.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Gold mining cost inflation is now a basket of energy-derived industrial inputs — track ammonia and aluminium alongside diesel as leading indicators of AISC.
insights.locator: Disruption to natural gas and ammonia markets

themes.theme: Scale and hedging as a moat

insights.claim: Major and intermediate gold producers were largely insulated from the March 2026 energy price spike through fuel inventories, hedging, power purchase agreements and long-term procurement, while junior counterparts were exposed.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Procurement scale is a real, quantifiable moat in an energy shock — favour majors over juniors while the Iran disruption persists.
insights.quote: Major and intermediate producers were mostly insulated from the March price volatility through fuel inventories, hedging, power purchase agreements and long-term procurement arrangements.
insights.locator: Major and intermediate producers were mostly insulated

insights.claim: OceanaGold, whose diesel is around 6% of AISC, had roughly 80% of annual fuel consumption hedged, limiting the immediate cost effect of the oil price move.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Disclosed fuel-hedge ratios and diesel-as-%-of-AISC are the two screening variables that separate protected producers from exposed ones this cycle.
insights.quote: around 80% of annual consumption was hedged
insights.locator: OceanaGold, whose diesel costs make up around 6% of AISC

insights.claim: Evolution Mining's existing fuel contracts prevented any operational disruption and Newmont avoided fuel shortages by leveraging scale and supplier relationships during the Q1'26 shock.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Named evidence that the majors' Q1 cost beats were procurement-driven and therefore temporary — do not extrapolate their cost outperformance past contract roll-off.
insights.locator: For example, Evolution Mining noted in its Q1’26 release

insights.claim: OceanaGold, Newmont and several other producers warned that a prolonged period of elevated fuel prices could have a materially greater cost impact in future quarters.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: The hedges are a delay, not a defence — position for a step-change in reported AISC when Q1 fuel contracts and hedges expire.
insights.quote: a prolonged period of elevated fuel prices could have a greater impact in future quarters
insights.locator: Nevertheless, OceanaGold, Newmont and several other producers cautioned

insights.claim: Spot gold momentarily hit US$5,595/oz in January 2026 and Q1'26 recorded by far the highest quarterly average nominal gold price on record, with the average price up 17% q/q and 70% y/y.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: The 70% y/y move is the anchor for every Q1'26 miner earnings comparison — base effects alone make H2'26 y/y growth far harder to sustain.
insights.quote: Spot gold prices reached unprecedented new highs, momentarily hitting US$5,595/oz in January, while Q1’26 recorded by far the highest quarterly average nominal price on record.
insights.locator: Spot gold prices reached unprecedented new highs

insights.claim: Average AISC margins rose 25% q/q and 134% y/y to a record US$3,076/oz in Q1'26, as the gold price increase far outstripped cost inflation.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: A margin more than double the year-ago level is the core bull case for gold equities — but it is the level to watch for mean reversion as prices fall and costs rise.
insights.quote: average AISC margins rose by 25% q/q and 134% y/y to a record US$3,076/oz
insights.locator: Record Margins and Cash Generation

insights.claim: High-cost producers at the 90th percentile of the cost curve saw AISC margins grow fastest, up 32% q/q to US$2,363/oz — outpacing the 25% industry average gain.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: The high-cost tail carries the greatest operating leverage in both directions — attractive on rallies, first to break on a sustained gold price decline.
insights.quote: Producers at the 90th percentile of the cost curve experienced particularly strong growth, with their AISC margins increasing by 32% q/q to US$2,363/oz.
insights.locator: Producers at the 90th percentile of the cost curve

insights.claim: Unlike previous gold booms, producers have kept relatively strict capital and cost discipline, leaving a host of them in net cash positions and returning a significant share of cash flow via dividends and buybacks.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: The absence of the classic boom-time overbuild means gold equities can be underwritten on cash return rather than growth capex — a genuine break from prior cycles.
insights.quote: In contrast to previous booms, gold miners have maintained relatively strict capital and cost discipline and so a host of producers now find themselves in net cash positions.
insights.locator: In contrast to previous booms

insights.claim: Newmont generated its highest ever quarterly free cash flow of US$3.1bn, returned US$2.7bn to shareholders and approved an additional US$6.0bn share buyback programme in Q1'26.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Returning ~87% of record FCF plus a US$6bn incremental buyback sets the capital-return benchmark peers will be measured against.
insights.locator: For example, Newmont returned US$2.7bn to shareholders

insights.claim: AngloGold Ashanti generated record free cash flow of US$1.2bn, moved from net debt into net cash, and raised its interim dividend to US$1.14/share from US$0.125/share in Q1'25 — a more than ninefold increase.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Dividend growth of this magnitude re-rates gold miners into an income story, widening the potential buyer base beyond commodity funds.
insights.locator: AngloGold Ashanti also generated record FCF

insights.claim: Average gold prices in Q2'26 were 7.2% lower q/q after the January peak, but remained well supported above US$4,000/oz.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: US$4,000/oz is the support level being treated as the operative floor — a break below it would turn a margin trim into a margin problem across the cost curve.
insights.quote: In Q2’26, average prices were 7.2% lower q/q, but remained well supported above US$4,000/oz.
insights.locator: Outlook

insights.claim: Because most of the Iran escalation occurred late in Q1'26, the full cost impact on fuel, freight and consumables should only become apparent in Q2'26 results — hitting margins at the same time as lower realised prices.
insights.speaker: Oliver Blagden
insights.so_what: Q2'26 is set up as a double squeeze: falling revenue per ounce plus the delayed cost shock — expect the first negative AISC surprises and guidance revisions of the cycle.
insights.quote: Given that much of the escalation occurred late in Q1’26, the full impact on fuel, freight and consumable costs is likely to become more apparent during Q2’26, placing additional pressure on margins.
insights.locator: Looking ahead, the industry’s resilience may be tested
